Some of the ACT NW (Nuclear Weapons) verification activities where SDF could contribute are: • Clearing a room: In this task, a SDF platform could explore a site or enclosure (room / warehouse / vehicle) to ensure that it contains no radiological sources. In such a scenario, information barriers are not needed, and the full richness of the dataset can be revealed to an inspector. Further the ability to move the SDF platform in 3D (i.e., randomly sample the radiation field in 3D space) can allow a thorough check and remove concerns arising from shielding of radiation sources. • Counting NW in an enclosure: In this setting, an enclosure is declared to contain M radiation sources and verification ensures that M is the correct number. In this scenario, information barriers would have to be active when the rich, multimodal measurements are collected and processed. The algorithms that extract sensitive information from the measurements and then reduce them to non-sensitive counts and information-poor summaries (e.g., 1D profiles of radiation intensities) would have to reside on the hidden side of the information barrier. These behind-the-barrier (computational) tasks would likely consist of reconstructing the radiation source field and then perhaps count the sources via hypothesis testing or model selection. This can be assisted if there is a map of radiation hot spots at a site. A SDF platform, which may reside at the facility and may produce data subjected to an information barrier, could be used to construct such a map. In such a case, the sensors and reconstruction algorithms could be supplied by the inspector while the computing platform and data-storage, where the sensitive data (and inferred information) would be created and stored, and which would exist on the hidden side of the information barrier, could be supplied by the inspected entity.
